description.text: Robert Bellarmine was born on 4 October 1542 in Montepulciano, Italy, and entered the Jesuit novitiate in 1560. He rose through the ranks of the Society of Jesus to become a professor of theology, rector of the Roman College, and in 1602 Archbishop of Capua. Bellarmine was a central figure in the Counter‑Reformation, supporting the decrees of the Council of Trent and playing a decisive role in the trials of Giordano Bruno and Galileo, as well as in the controversy with King James I of England.

Beyond his ecclesiastical duties, Bellarmine was a prolific writer and scholar. He authored the extensive *Disputationes de controversiis christianae fidei*, a systematic defense of Catholic doctrine against Protestant arguments, and a catechism approved by Pope Clement VIII. He also composed hymns, including one on Mary Magdalene that entered the Roman Breviary, and wrote a Hebrew grammar. Bellarmine was canonized in 1930 and declared a Doctor of the Church in 1931, cementing his legacy as a leading theologian of his era.

curiosities.text: Bellarmine was the first Jesuit to teach at the University of Leuven, where he lectured on Thomas Aquinas’s *Summa Theologica* and earned a reputation as a rigorous scholar.
He wrote a Hebrew grammar, a rare achievement for a Catholic theologian of the 16th century, reflecting his broad linguistic interests.

Bellarmine authored a certificate for Galileo in 1616 that clarified the Church’s position on the Copernican system, allowing Galileo to continue teaching the mathematical aspects of heliocentrism as a theoretical tool.
He composed a hymn on Mary Magdalene that was included in the Roman Breviary, demonstrating his contribution to Catholic liturgical music.
Bellarmine’s *Disputationes* was briefly placed on the Index of Forbidden Books in 1590 by Pope Sixtus V, only to be removed from the Index during the brief reign of Pope Urban VII.
